cases.title: Tax Reform or Privilege?
cases.mission: Evaluate resistance to taxation and privilege.
cases.scenario: A finance minister says, "We must tax the nobility and the church to pay our huge state debts." A nobleman replies, "Our ancient rights protect us from new taxes, so only an Estates-General can approve them."
notes: By 1788, half of state revenue went on servicing its debt because France primarily used loans to fund wars.
The nobility and the Church benefited from a variety of tax exemptions while the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes.
New tax laws had to be registered with regional judicial bodies or parlements that were able to block them.
The Assembly of Notables and parlements argued that proposed taxes could only be approved by an Estates-General.
Public opinion was firmly on the side of the parlements, and riots broke out in several towns.

idea: France faced a massive debt crisis in the eighteenth century.
The nobility and the church paid almost no taxes.
Reform attempts were blocked by regional judicial bodies.
This political impasse led to the calling of the Estates-General.
reading.example: The finance minister proposed a universal land tax, but the assembly of notables rejected it.
key_words: a regional judicial body that registered laws
a representative body of the three estates
freedom from an obligation like paying taxes
reading.think: Why might privileged groups resist paying taxes even during a state financial crisis?

nodes.label: Heavy state debt
nodes.quote: France primarily used loans to fund the 1778 to 1783 Anglo-French War. Even after it ended, the monarchy continued to borrow heavily, and by 1788, half of state revenue went on servicing its debt.

nodes.label: Unequal tax burden
nodes.quote: As the nobility and Church benefited from a variety of exemptions, the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes.

nodes.label: Parlements block laws
nodes.quote: Reform was difficult because new tax laws had to be registered with regional judicial bodies or parlements that were able to block them.

nodes.label: Estates-General demand
nodes.quote: The notables and parlements argued that the proposed taxes could only be approved by an Estates-General, a representative body that last met in 1614.

nodes.label: Public support riots
nodes.quote: Public opinion was firmly on the side of the parlements, and riots broke out in several towns.

nodes.text: Brienne announced that the king would summon an Estates-General to convene the following May after his loans failed.
nodes.label: Summoning Estates-General
nodes.quote: Brienne's attempts to raise new loans failed, and on 8 August 1788, he announced that the king would summon an Estates-General to convene the following May.

nodes.text: Resistance to reform by the ruling elite made the state unable to manage its financial crisis.
nodes.label: Elite resistance
nodes.quote: Combined with resistance to reform by the ruling elite and indecisive policy by king Louis XVI and his ministers, the result was a crisis the state was unable to manage.

t128f4fee7e:ind-fact.situation: In 1787, the Assembly of Notables rejected new taxes. In 1788, regional parlements blocked reforms. In several towns, riots broke out against royal edicts.

t128f4fee7e:ind-caus.situation: Huge state debts led to demands for tax reform. Tax exemptions led to financial collapse. Blocked reforms led to widespread public riots.
t128f4fee7e:ind-caus.question: What general cause and effect pattern links these three situations?

t128f4fee7e:ind-rela.situation: As state debt grew larger, tax demands increased. As noble resistance grew stronger, public riots spread across several French towns.

t128f4fee7e:ded-conc.situation: The nobility possessed legal tax exemptions under the old regime. A nobleman owns large estates in the countryside.
t128f4fee7e:ded-conc.question: How does the concept of privilege apply to this nobleman tax status?

t128f4fee7e:ded-proc.situation: New tax laws required registration with regional parlements before taking effect. The king issues a new property tax decree.
t128f4fee7e:ded-proc.question: What exact steps must happen next for this tax decree to become legal?

t128f4fee7e:ded-caus.situation: Tax exemptions for the rich forced the lower classes to bear the entire financial burden.

t128f4fee7e:ded-rela.situation: Regional parlements blocked royal taxes to protect their status. The central government needed money urgently.
t128f4fee7e:ded-rela.question: How does the blockage by parlements affect the state debt crisis?

t128f4fee7e:abd-fact.situation: Riots suddenly broke out in several French towns after the parlements rejected the new royal tax edicts.

t128f4fee7e:abd-conc.situation: Nobles fiercely defended their ancient rights while ordinary people paid heavy taxes with no political voice.

t128f4fee7e:abd-proc.situation: The finance minister failed to pass tax reform through the assembly and parlements before riots started.
t128f4fee7e:abd-proc.question: What alternative method should the minister have used to avoid this outcome?

t128f4fee7e:abd-caus.situation: Public opinion strongly supported the parlements against the king even though the parlements protected noble tax privileges.
t128f4fee7e:abd-caus.question: What underlying reason explains why ordinary citizens supported the wealthy parlements?

t128f4fee7e:abd-rela.situation: Regional parlements gained massive popularity among citizens by blocking the king tax proposals.
t128f4fee7e:abd-rela.question: What is the most likely link between parlement resistance and the rise of revolutionary spirit?

cases.title: Good motive or murder?
cases.mission: Tell euthanasia apart from murder by checking intent.
cases.scenario: A man kills his sick relative to end their pain. A critic says, "This is just murder because he ended a life."
notes: The British House of Lords select committee on medical ethics defines euthanasia as a deliberate intervention undertaken with the express intention of ending a life to relieve intractable suffering.
Intentionality distinguishes euthanasia from intentional killing because the agent must have a good motive for the person killed.
A person must first identify whether the act was done with the express intention to relieve pain.
A good motive leads to a merciful death rather than personal gain, so the action counts as euthanasia.
Commentators argue that killing for personal gain is murder rather than euthanasia.

idea: Euthanasia means ending a life to relieve pain.
Different groups define it using different rules.
Intent and motive are central to the definition.
Killing for personal gain is always murder.
reading.example: A doctor gives a lethal dose to stop endless pain.
key_words: intentionally ending life to eliminate pain and suffering
the reason why a person performs an action
illegal killing without a merciful motive
reading.think: What makes an action euthanasia instead of murder?

nodes.label: House of Lords definition
nodes.quote: a deliberate intervention undertaken with the express intention of ending a life to relieve intractable suffering

nodes.label: Motive matters
nodes.quote: the principal thing that distinguishes euthanasia from intentional killing simpliciter is the agent's motive: it must be a good motive insofar as the good of the person killed is concerned

nodes.label: Check the intent

nodes.text: Heather Draper argued that euthanasia requires an agent, a subject, an intention, causal proximity, and an outcome.
nodes.label: Draper elements
nodes.quote: death that results from the intention of one person to kill another person, using the most gentle and painless means possible, that is motivated solely by the best interests of the person who dies

nodes.text: Michael Wreen offered a definition requiring that the killing is voluntary and motivated by the good of the person.
nodes.label: Wreen definition

nodes.text: Beauchamp and Davidson stated that the death must be intended by another human being to be an instance of euthanasia.
nodes.label: Intended death

nodes.text: Definitions must exclude killing for personal gain to avoid labeling crimes as euthanasia.
nodes.label: Exclude personal gain

cases.title: Hard law or soft law?
cases.mission: Compare hard laws and soft rules for AI.
cases.scenario: A tech executive says, "We do not need hard laws for AI because fast-moving technology needs flexible soft law approaches instead."
notes: Regulation of artificial intelligence is the development of public sector policies and laws for promoting and regulating artificial intelligence.
Hard law approaches to AI regulation have substantial challenges because AI technology is rapidly evolving.
Soft law approaches to AI regulation are promising because they offer greater flexibility to adapt to emerging technologies.
Soft law approaches often lack substantial enforcement potential.
Organizations deploying AI have a central role to play in creating and implementing trustworthy AI.

idea: AI regulation involves public sector policies and laws.
Hard laws struggle to keep pace with fast changes.
Soft laws offer flexibility but lack enforcement.
Organizations must also take accountability for AI risks.
reading.example: A company uses voluntary ethics guidelines instead of waiting for a government statute.
key_words: binding legal rules with strict penalties
guidelines and voluntary standards without direct legal force
reading.think: How can rules keep up with fast technology?

cases.title: Governing agentic AI?
cases.mission: Analyze challenges in regulating autonomous AI agents.
cases.scenario: A policy advisor argues, "Standard generative AI rules will work fine for new autonomous AI agents without needing changes."
notes: Agentic AI regulation is in early stages compared to generative AI systems.
AI agents are more complex, more autonomous, and have less human oversight.
AI agents can work with multiple actors within multiple systems, making regulation more difficult.
Gardhouse et al. argue that AI agents have too many dynamic variables to have specific regulations based on fixed points in time.
One approach is to have other deep learning systems or AI agents specifically monitor subsequent AI agents as an oversight measure.

idea: AI agents act with high autonomy across multiple systems.
Traditional rules made for simple chatbots fail here.
Dynamic variables prevent fixed point regulations.
Using other AI systems to monitor agents is one proposed solution.
reading.example: An AI assistant books flights, negotiates prices, and coordinates schedules across apps without asking first.
key_words: an artificial intelligence system that acts independently to achieve goals
factors that change constantly over time
reading.think: How do you oversee software that runs by itself?

cases.title: Controlling inflation
cases.mission: Examine how central banks manage inflation today.
cases.scenario: A news anchor says, "The central bank must raise interest rates now to keep inflation low and stable."
notes: Today, most economists favour a low and steady rate of inflation.
Low inflation reduces the likelihood of economic recessions by enabling the labor market to adjust.
The task of keeping the rate of inflation low and stable is usually given to central banks.
Central banks control monetary policy normally through the setting of interest rates.
Since the 1980s, inflation has been held low and stable in countries with independent central banks.

idea: Uncontrolled inflation or deflation can harm a country's economy.
To prevent this, nations give central banks the job of keeping prices stable.
Central banks use monetary policy tools like interest rates to guide the economy.
Keeping inflation low and steady helps avoid big economic crises.
reading.example: When a central bank raises interest rates, borrowing becomes costlier, which can help cool down fast-rising prices.
key_words: a national bank that manages monetary policy and interest rates
the amount charged for borrowing money
actions taken by a central bank to influence the economy's money supply
reading.think: How might changing interest rates affect the choices people make about spending and saving money?

cases.topic: The Science and Definition of Love
cases.title: Stages of Love
cases.mission: Understand the biological stages of romance.
cases.scenario: Your friend has been dating someone for a few weeks and says, "We have so much passion and energy, so this intense excitement will surely last forever."
notes: Lust is the initial passionate sexual desire that promotes mating, and involves the increased release of hormones such as testosterone and estrogen.
These effects rarely last more than a few weeks or months.
Attraction is the more individualized and romantic desire for a specific candidate for mating, which develops out of lust.
Biological models view romantic love as a mammalian drive or motivation system, much like hunger or thirst.
First, identify the current stage of the relationship, then compare it with known biological timelines before expecting permanent excitement.

idea: Love involves distinct biological stages.
Lust and attraction use up specific body chemicals.
These early stages are temporary.
Long term bonds need different systems.
reading.example: A couple feels intense excitement at first, but this feeling changes over the years.
key_words: initial passionate sexual desire that promotes mating
individualized and romantic desire for a specific candidate
bonding that promotes relationships lasting for many years
reading.think: Why do intense early feelings often fade over time?

cases.topic: The Science and Definition of Love
cases.title: Triangular Theory
cases.mission: Identify different components of love in relationships.
cases.scenario: Your sibling says, "True love is only about deep passion, so if the excitement drops, the relationship is over."
notes: Psychologist Robert Sternberg formulated a triangular theory of love in which love has three components: intimacy, commitment, and passion.
Intimacy is when two people share confidences and various details of their personal lives.
Commitment is the expectation that the relationship is permanent.
All forms of love are viewed as varying combinations of these three components.
First, list the presence of intimacy, passion, and commitment, then classify the relationship type based on these three parts.

idea: Love has multiple dimensions beyond simple passion.
Intimacy involves sharing personal details.
Commitment means expecting a permanent bond.
Different relationships combine these parts differently.
reading.example: A couple may have high commitment and intimacy even when daily passion changes.
key_words: sharing confidences and personal details with another person
the expectation that a relationship is permanent
romantic and sexual excitement in a relationship
reading.think: Can a relationship survive without passion if it has intimacy and commitment?

cases.topic: The Science and Definition of Love
cases.title: Love as Action
cases.mission: Evaluate love as a commitment rather than just a feeling.
cases.scenario: A colleague says, "Love is just a passing emotion, so you cannot choose to love someone if the feeling goes away."
notes: Erich Fromm maintained in his book The Art of Loving that love is not merely a feeling but is also actions.
Fromm described love as a conscious choice that in its early stages might originate as an involuntary feeling.
Love later no longer depends on those feelings, but rather depends only on conscious commitment.
St. Thomas Aquinas defines love as to will the good of another.
First, observe the ongoing actions towards another person, then evaluate the conscious commitment behind those actions.

idea: Love involves deliberate actions over time.
Feelings of love can start automatically.
Sustained love relies on conscious commitment.
Willing the good of another is central.
reading.example: A person cares for a sick partner daily, regardless of temporary emotional fluctuations.
key_words: adherence to loving actions towards another over a sustained duration
doing things that actively support the well being of another
an emotional state that can change quickly
